name: Ivan Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a one-man translation business, Russian and Ukrainian into English, mostly shipping contracts, cargo papers and some online shop listings. My whole set-up runs on AI: it drafts, I check and fix, and I can turn round in a day what used to take a week. I live with my grandmother in her flat above the old ferry office, because she needs help and the rent is low. Every spare penny goes back into the business: software, a proper website, a stamp for certified work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Growing, slowly. I've got two shipping agents at the port who send me something most weeks. The problem is that I reinvest everything, so I've got about ten days of money in the bank, and a shipping agent can take sixty days to pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, then I keep my edge. The people who learned the tools are ahead of those who didn't, and that doesn't change. I'd post about how my turnaround beats any agency in the region.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for me. My business works because the tools are good but not good enough to replace me. If it stays like that, I grow. My only worry is cash, because I keep spending on the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep growing: one more shipping client by spring and a third agent at the port. I'd stop buying new software for six months and build a cushion of one month. And I'd think about taking on a part-time checker, maybe a student, once the work is steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, mostly. The cash flow makes me twitchy, but that's what building something feels like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why reinvest everything instead of saving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my grandfather ran a fishing boat. My grandfather always said you don't get a bigger boat by keeping the money in a sock. My grandmother says my grandfather also nearly lost the boat twice. They're both right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would that part-time checker be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a Ukrainian student from the college who needs work. Someone who knows the language and wants to learn the trade. I'd rather train someone than wait for the government to.

My **turnaround** beats any agency in the region.
think: My business works because the tools are **good, not good enough**.
My only worry is **cash**, because I reinvest everything.
do: Win **one more shipping client** by spring.
Stop buying **software** for six months to build a cushion.
Take on a **part-time checker** once work is steady.
feel: **Good, mostly**, with cash flow making him twitchy.

fieldNote: He's a **builder**: AI is the engine of his one-man business.
Free-market outlook, with a **family** lesson behind it.

steps.text: Win a third shipping agent at the port by spring
Stop new software spending for six months to build a cushion
Hire a Ukrainian college student as a part-time checker

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the market doing what it does, and people who move fast will be fine. I'd say it at the port and online. I wouldn't ask anyone for help; I'd ask for customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it cuts both ways. I'd win work from slow agencies, but the shipping agents might start doing their own translations with the same tools. I'd need to offer something they can't easily do themselves, like the certified stamp and the responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell a package: AI drafting, my check and my stamp, at a fixed monthly price. I'd chase the slower agencies' clients in the first six months. And I'd build an app for the shipping agents that pre-fills cargo papers, so I'm part of their system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly. Some fear, because the floor moves, but more excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who loses if you win?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older translators at the agency in town, probably. That's hard to say out loud. But the market rewards the person who adapts, and I'd rather be him than them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the shipping agents cut you out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be in trouble quickly with ten days of money. So I'd tie them in with a contract and the stamp. Nobody wants to be the one who signed a bad cargo paper. That's why the shipping agents still need my stamp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or go under, and I'd mean it for myself too. I'd tell other small business people not to wait for the government. I'd say families need to stick together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my business is a middleman, and AGI cuts out middlemen first. If the AI can do the checking and the shipping agents trust it, I'm finished in a year. The robots in 2031 don't help me, because there's nothing physical in what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year squeezing as much work as I can while clients still want a human signature. I'd save every penny for once. Then I'd look at the port itself, maybe buying into a small cargo handling or boat repair business, where hands-on work lasts until about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'm usually the one who sees change coming, but two years is not time to build anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying into a business with ten days of money. How?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With my uncle. Uncle Sergei has a boat repair yard at the port and wants to retire. I'd put in what I save from the translation work and he'd let me pay the rest over time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your grandmother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She stays with me, whatever happens. That's not negotiable. If money got tight, we'd cut everything else first.

fieldNote: Even an **adaptive entrepreneur** sees his business vanish quickly here.
Uses **family business** at the port as his hands-on exit.

steps.text: Take every certified job while clients still want a human signature
Save every penny from translation for one year
Buy into uncle Sergei's boat repair yard on staged payments
Leave translation for the boat repair yard

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a business plan, not a disaster. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen: start now, and you'll be fine. I'd keep it upbeat in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd have three good years, maybe four, then translation goes. I'd want to sell the business or wind it down by year four. I'd need somewhere to land, and I'd need savings, which I've never had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow fast in years one and two, take on a checker and build up a client list worth something. Then I'd try to sell the client list to a bigger agency. I'd put the money and my savings into the boat repair yard with uncle Sergei by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but in a way I like. It's a race and I've got a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would buy a translation client list if everyone knows AGI is coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good question. Nobody buys a translation client list in year four. I'd have to sell in year two or three, while people still think they have time. Timing is everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the boat yard a long-term answer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, robots come for boat repair by 2034. But it gives me three more years and something physical I own. And people with boats always want someone they trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone who'll work. I'd tell young people to learn a trade and use the tools at the same time. I'd be fairly loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have six or seven very good years, maybe the best of my life, before translation fades. I'd build the business, sell it while it's worth something, and move into the yard. I'd be 33 or 34 when I switch, which is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hire two checkers and grow into the shipping trade properly. I'd save a set share every month for the first time. Around 2032 I'd sell up and move into boat repair with my uncle, maybe adding AI to run the yard's bookings and parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly confident. A bit watchful, because plans always meet surprises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'for anyone who'll work'. Who wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People who want someone else to fix it for them. My grandmother came here with one suitcase and built a life. Ten years is a lot more than my grandmother had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything worry you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd get comfortable and miss the moment to sell. Ten years makes people lazy. I'd write the date on the wall.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time to sell and no savings to fall back on. What would help is easy small business loans and simpler rules for buying into a family business, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who I'm doing it for. I'm not just taking risks for me. I'm taking risks for my grandmother and one day a family of my own.

headlineQuote: I'm not just taking risks for me. I'm taking risks for my grandmother and one day a family of my own.
portrait: Ivan is a **27-year-old** Russian and Ukrainian translator running a **one-man AI-powered** business at the port.
He lives with and cares for his **grandmother**, and reinvests every spare penny.
Free-market and self-reliant, he sees AI as a **tool for growth**, not a threat.
In fast scenarios he expects his middleman business to vanish and plans a move into his **uncle's boat yard**.
With more time he plans to **grow, sell and exit**, fearing only his own complacency.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time to sell the business and no savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Small business loans** and simpler rules for buying into a family business.
